What Is Memory?

Memory is not a single thing — it is a set of mental processes that allow us to take in information, hold it, and use it later. Psychologists break this down into three key processes: encoding, storage, and retrieval. Understanding how each works helps explain why we sometimes remember things perfectly and why at other times information seems to vanish.

Key Fact

Memory works through three processes: encoding (converting input into a storable form), storage (holding the information), and retrieval (getting the information back out). Without all three, a memory cannot be used.

Encoding: Getting Information In

Encoding is the first step in forming a memory. When you encounter something — a name, a fact, a smell — your brain converts it into a format that can be stored. Information can be encoded in different ways: visually (as an image), acoustically (as a sound or word in your head), or semantically (by meaning). For example, if you are introduced to someone called Mia, you might encode her name by how it sounds, what it means, or by associating it with something you already know.

The type of encoding matters. Deeper, more meaningful encoding tends to result in stronger, longer-lasting memories. Surface encoding — simply repeating something without thinking about what it means — produces weaker memories that fade more quickly.

Storage and Retrieval

Storage refers to keeping the information in the memory system. Information does not simply sit in a single place — different types of memory are stored in different ways and in different parts of the system. Retrieval is the process of getting information back out when you need it. Even if information is stored, retrieval can fail — for example, the “tip-of-the-tongue” experience shows that information may be stored but temporarily hard to retrieve.

Retrieval failure happens when information has been stored but cannot be accessed at that moment. This can occur because the right retrieval cue is missing — a trigger such as a context, smell, or related word that helps unlock the memory. Without the cue, the memory stays out of reach. Retrieval failures can also happen when competing memories interfere with each other, a process called interference that is covered in detail in a later lesson.

Types of Long-Term Memory

Psychologists distinguish three types of long-term memory. Each stores a different kind of information and works in a slightly different way. It is important to learn these carefully — students frequently mix them up, particularly procedural and episodic memory.

Key Fact

The three types of long-term memory are: episodic (personal events tied to a time and place), semantic (general knowledge and facts), and procedural (how to perform learned skills). Procedural memory operates largely without conscious recall.

Episodic Memory

Episodic memory is your personal autobiography — the record of events you have directly experienced. These memories are tied to a specific time and place. Examples include remembering your first day at secondary school, what you had for breakfast this morning, or a birthday party from last year. Episodic memories are conscious and can be deliberately recalled; they also feel personal because they belong to your own life story.

Semantic Memory

Semantic memory holds your general knowledge about the world — facts, meanings, concepts, and language. Knowing that Paris is the capital of France, that water boils at 100°C, or what the word “democracy” means are all examples of semantic memory. Unlike episodic memories, semantic memories are not tied to a particular personal experience. You know that water boils at 100°C but you probably cannot recall the specific moment you learned it.

Procedural Memory

Procedural memory is memory for how to do things. Riding a bike, typing, tying your shoelaces, playing a musical instrument — all of these rely on procedural memory. A key feature is that procedural memory operates largely automatically, without needing to consciously think through the steps. This is why expert performers often say they do not consciously think about what they are doing; the skill runs on procedural memory.

Episodic memory is conscious and personal — it requires you to mentally travel back to a specific past experience. Semantic memory is also conscious and can be deliberately recalled, but it has no personal “time stamp.” Procedural memory is typically unconscious and automatic; once a skill is well learned, it no longer requires deliberate attention. The most common confusion is between episodic and procedural memory: episodic is WHAT happened to you; procedural is HOW to do a skill. Knowing you once learned to ride a bike is episodic; the ability to ride it without thinking is procedural.

The Multi-Store Model

Where does a memory go after you first encounter it? The multi-store model of memory proposes that information travels through three distinct stores: the sensory register, short-term memory, and long-term memory. Each store differs in how it codes information, how much it can hold (capacity), and how long it retains information (duration).

Key Fact

The multi-store model has three stores: the sensory register (large capacity, very brief duration), short-term memory (limited capacity of about 7 items, up to about 30 seconds), and long-term memory (potentially unlimited capacity, potentially permanent duration).

The Sensory Register

The sensory register receives information from all your senses simultaneously. It has a very large capacity — it can hold a huge amount of incoming sensory data — but its duration is extremely brief, lasting only fractions of a second. Most information in the sensory register is never processed further and simply fades away. Only information that is attended to moves on to short-term memory.

The coding in the sensory register matches the sense that detected it: visual information is coded visually (iconic memory), and auditory information is coded acoustically (echoic memory). Think of the brief afterimage you see when someone takes a flash photograph — that flicker of visual information is your iconic sensory register in action.

Short-Term Memory

Short-term memory (STM) holds information that is currently in use — for example, a phone number you have just read or the words in the sentence you are reading right now. STM has a limited capacity: research suggests around 7 items, plus or minus 2. Its duration is also limited — without rehearsal, information in STM lasts only around 15 to 30 seconds before it fades. The coding in STM is primarily acoustic — we tend to hold information as sounds in our head, even when we read written words silently.

Rehearsal is the key mechanism for transferring information from STM to long-term memory. By repeating or thinking about information, you keep it active in STM and eventually strengthen it enough to be stored long-term. Without rehearsal, information in STM decays and is lost. This is why repeating a phone number to yourself works — until you stop rehearsing, it stays available.

Long-Term Memory

Long-term memory (LTM) is the relatively permanent store for information that has passed through STM. Its capacity is thought to be essentially unlimited — there is no known upper bound on how much LTM can hold. Duration can be extremely long; people retain memories for their entire lifetime. The coding in LTM is primarily semantic — information is stored in terms of its meaning rather than its sound or appearance.

Key Fact

STM codes mainly acoustically, holds about 7 items (±2), and lasts up to around 30 seconds without rehearsal. LTM codes mainly semantically, has potentially unlimited capacity, and can last a lifetime.

A strength of the multi-store model is that it is supported by research. For example, Murdock’s serial position curve study (covered in the next lesson) provides evidence for the distinction between STM (recency effect) and LTM (primacy effect). The model also generates clear, testable predictions about coding, capacity and duration.

A weakness is that the model may be oversimplified. It treats STM and LTM as single, unitary stores, but later research suggests both are more complex. For instance, long-term memory is divided into episodic, semantic and procedural memory (as you saw in Lesson 1). The model also suggests rehearsal is the only route to LTM, but we know that emotionally significant events can enter LTM even without deliberate rehearsal.

How Information Moves Between Stores

Understanding the flow of information through the multi-store model is as important as knowing the features of each store. Information first reaches the sensory register automatically and simultaneously from all active sense organs. At any given moment, your sensory register holds a vast amount of information — every sound in the room, every patch of colour in your visual field, every sensation on your skin. Nearly all of this is never consciously attended to and fades within fractions of a second.

The gateway between the sensory register and STM is attention. When you selectively attend to a piece of incoming sensory information — for example, you hear your name mentioned in a noisy room — it is transferred into STM and becomes available for conscious processing. Everything else in the sensory register is lost without ever being consciously registered.

Once information is in STM, rehearsal determines whether it passes into LTM. Maintenance rehearsal — simply repeating information — keeps it circulating in STM. With sufficient repetition, the trace is strengthened enough to be stored in LTM as a more permanent memory. Without rehearsal, STM traces decay within about 30 seconds and are gone. This explains why you can forget a phone number almost immediately if you are interrupted before you dial it.

Not all information enters LTM only through deliberate rehearsal. Elaborative rehearsal — thinking deeply about meaning and linking new information to what you already know — is more effective than simple repetition. Emotionally significant events can also bypass ordinary rehearsal and enter LTM rapidly, which is why flashbulb memories (such as exactly where you were when you heard dramatic news) can be so vivid and lasting even without conscious rehearsal.

Serial Position and Recall

If someone reads you a list of twenty words and asks you to recall them in any order, the position of each word in the list affects how likely you are to remember it. This is called the serial position effect. Psychologists have found two consistent patterns in this effect: you tend to remember words at the beginning of the list (the primacy effect) and words at the end of the list (the recency effect) better than words in the middle.

Key Fact

The primacy effect refers to better recall of items at the start of a list; the recency effect refers to better recall of items at the end. The primacy effect is explained by transfer to long-term memory via rehearsal; the recency effect is explained by items still being active in short-term memory.

The Primacy Effect

The primacy effect occurs because the first few items on a list receive the most rehearsal. When you hear the first word, there is nothing else competing for your attention in short-term memory, so you repeat it several times. By the time the list is over, those early words have been rehearsed enough to be transferred into long-term memory, where they can be retrieved later. Words in the middle of the list receive less rehearsal because STM is quickly filled by new incoming items.

The Recency Effect

The recency effect occurs because the last few words on the list are the most recently heard and are still being held in short-term memory at the time of recall. They have not had time to fade. However, the recency effect is fragile: if there is a delay before recall, or if participants are asked to do a distracting task between hearing the list and recalling it, the recency effect disappears because STM trace has faded. The primacy effect remains because those early words are safely in LTM.

When psychologists plot the probability of recall against the position of each word in a list, the result is a U-shaped graph called the serial position curve. Recall is high for the first few words (primacy), drops in the middle, and rises again for the last few words (recency). This characteristic shape appears consistently across many free recall studies.

Murdock’s Serial Position Curve Study

The most important study in this area is Murdock’s (1962) investigation of the serial position effect. It is a named study you need to know in detail: aim, method, results, and conclusion.

Key Fact

Murdock (1962): Aim — to investigate the serial position effect in free recall. Method — participants heard lists of words at a set rate and were asked to recall them in any order immediately after. Results — words at the start (primacy) and end (recency) were recalled better than words in the middle; a U-shaped serial position curve was produced. Conclusion — the pattern supports the idea of separate STM and LTM stores.

A strength of Murdock’s study is that it used a controlled laboratory method, which allows replication and high internal validity — extraneous variables such as word length and presentation rate were carefully controlled. The study produced consistent, replicable results that have been repeated many times, supporting its reliability.

A weakness is that the task was artificial: memorising lists of unrelated words has little resemblance to everyday memory tasks. This reduces ecological validity — results may not reflect how memory works in real life. The study also used participants in a restricted setting, which may limit how far findings generalise to all people and all types of memory task.

Link to the Multi-Store Model

The serial position curve provides evidence for the multi-store model of memory. The primacy effect demonstrates that rehearsal can transfer information into long-term memory — early items are recalled from LTM. The recency effect demonstrates the existence of a separate, limited short-term store — end items are recalled directly from STM. When a delay is introduced before recall, the recency effect disappears but the primacy effect remains, which is exactly what the multi-store model would predict: STM traces fade quickly while LTM traces persist.

Why Middle Items Are Recalled Poorly

It is worth understanding precisely why items in the middle of a list are the hardest to recall. When you hear the first few words, your STM is relatively empty and you can rehearse them repeatedly. But as more words arrive, your STM fills to its limited capacity of around seven items. New words displace older ones before those older words have had enough rehearsal to reach LTM. At the same time, the middle items are not the most recent, so they are no longer active in STM at the point of recall. The result is that they fall through the gap between the two stores and are lost.

This competition between new and old items in a limited-capacity store is sometimes called displacement. Each new item in a full STM pushes out the item that has been there longest without sufficient rehearsal to move it to LTM. Middle items receive neither the rehearsal advantage of early items nor the recency advantage of final items, which is why the serial position curve dips in the middle.

The displacement account is consistent with the multi-store model’s claim that STM has a fixed capacity of around seven items (plus or minus two). If STM had unlimited capacity, every item would have as much opportunity for rehearsal as the first item, and there would be no primacy advantage — the serial position curve would be flat, not U-shaped.

Memory as an Active Process

You might assume that remembering is like playing back a recording — a faithful replay of what happened. But psychologists have found that memory is far more active than this. When we recall something, we do not simply read it out from storage; we actively reconstruct it, filling in gaps using our existing knowledge, expectations, and beliefs. This process can lead to errors, distortions, and even entirely false memories.

Bartlett’s Theory of Reconstructive Memory

Frederick Bartlett argued that memory is not a passive copy of the past but an active process of reconstruction. He proposed the concept of schema — a mental framework of knowledge built up from past experience. When we recall something, we use our schemas to fill in the gaps, making the memory fit what we “expect” to be true rather than what actually happened. Bartlett called this tendency effort after meaning: we work to make our memories logical and coherent, even if that means unconsciously altering them.

Key Fact

Bartlett’s Theory of Reconstructive Memory proposes that recall is an active reconstruction shaped by schemas and the effort after meaning. This explains why our recollections often change over time, filling in gaps to match what we expect rather than what actually occurred.

Bartlett’s War of the Ghosts Study

Bartlett tested his theory using a story called “The War of the Ghosts,” a Native American folk tale unfamiliar to his British participants. He chose this story deliberately because it contained cultural elements and a narrative logic that would be foreign to British readers, so any changes in retelling would reveal how schemas distort memory.

Key Fact

Bartlett’s War of the Ghosts study: Aim — to investigate how memory for an unfamiliar story changes over time. Method — British participants read the story and recalled it repeatedly over intervals ranging from hours to years. Results — participants altered, shortened and rationalised the story to fit familiar cultural expectations; unfamiliar elements were omitted or replaced. Conclusion — memory is an active reconstruction shaped by prior knowledge and schemas, not a faithful replay.

A strength of Bartlett’s study is its ecological validity — participants recalled a meaningful story rather than an artificial list of words, which is closer to real-world memory tasks. The repeated recall method also reveals how memory changes over time, which has practical implications for eyewitness testimony.

A weakness is that Bartlett’s methods were not tightly controlled. The story was not standardised in all versions, and Bartlett did not use statistical analysis — he relied on qualitative descriptions of changes. This makes it harder to replicate precisely and limits how confidently we can draw general conclusions from his data.

Factors Affecting the Accuracy of Memory

Beyond schemas, three specific factors can distort what we remember: interference, context, and false memories. Each operates differently, but all demonstrate that memory is not a fixed record.

Interference

Interference occurs when one memory makes another harder to recall or distorts it. There are two types. Proactive interference is when an older memory disrupts recall of a newer one — for example, if you have previously learned Spanish, it may interfere with learning Italian. Retroactive interference is when a newer memory disrupts recall of an older one — for example, if you learn a new phone number, it may make you more likely to forget your old one.

Context

Memory is also affected by context. Research has shown that memory is better when the conditions at retrieval match the conditions during encoding. This is known as context-dependent memory. For example, information learned in a particular room may be recalled more easily when you return to that room. Internal states can also act as context: if you encode a memory while in a particular emotional state, you may recall it more easily when you return to that state.

False Memories

False memories are recollections of events that either never happened or are substantially different from how they actually occurred. They can arise from post-event misinformation, suggestion from others, or the natural reconstructive processes Bartlett described. False memories feel just as real to the person holding them as genuine ones, which has significant implications for eyewitness testimony in legal settings.

Understanding that memory is reconstructive has important real-world implications. Eyewitness testimony is less reliable than courts once assumed, because witnesses unconsciously alter their memories using schemas, are affected by leading questions (post-event information), and may form false memories. Research in this area has influenced how police conduct interviews and how courts evaluate eyewitness evidence.

Sensation and Perception

When light enters your eye, your retina detects it. But detecting the light is not the same as understanding what you are looking at. Psychologists draw a crucial distinction between sensation and perception. Sensation is the physical detection of stimuli by the sense organs — it is passive and automatic. Perception is the brain’s active interpretation of those signals to create a meaningful experience of the world.

A simple example illustrates the difference: your eye detects a patch of reflected light (sensation), but your brain interprets it as a red apple sitting on a table (perception). The same raw data reaches the retina, but perception gives it meaning. This distinction matters because it opens the question of what shapes perception — is it driven mainly by the raw information available (as Gibson argued) or mainly by our prior knowledge and experience (as Gregory argued)?

Key Fact

Sensation is the passive detection of physical energy by sense organs. Perception is the brain’s active interpretation of that information to create a meaningful experience. All perception begins with sensation, but sensation alone is not perception.

Visual Cues and Depth Perception

One of the brain’s most impressive feats is judging distance and depth from the flat, two-dimensional images formed on the retina. It does this using depth cues. Some cues require only one eye (monocular depth cues); others require both eyes working together (binocular depth cues).

Monocular Depth Cues

Monocular depth cues can be detected with just one eye. There are four you need to know:

Height in plane — objects that appear higher in the visual field (closer to the horizon) are perceived as further away. Think of a field of people: those near the horizon appear in the upper part of your visual field and are seen as more distant.

Relative size — when two objects are known to be the same size, the one that projects a smaller image on the retina is perceived as further away. A friend who appears smaller in your view is interpreted as being further away, not as having physically shrunk.

Occlusion — when one object partially blocks another from view, the partially blocked object is perceived as further away. The blocking object is seen as being in front. This is one of the most reliable monocular cues.

Linear perspective — parallel lines (like railway tracks or a straight road) appear to converge at a distant vanishing point. The closer together the lines appear, the further away that part of the scene is judged to be.

Key Fact

The four monocular depth cues are: height in plane (higher in visual field = further), relative size (smaller image = further), occlusion (blocked object = further), and linear perspective (converging lines = further). These can all be detected with one eye.

Binocular Depth Cues

Binocular depth cues depend on having two eyes. Because our eyes are set a short distance apart, each eye receives a slightly different view of the same scene. The brain uses this difference to calculate depth.

Retinal disparity is the difference between the images received by the left and right eyes. Because the eyes are set apart, nearby objects create a larger difference between the two images than distant objects do. The brain uses the size of this disparity to calculate how far away an object is. Close objects have greater disparity; distant objects have less. You can experience this by holding a finger close to your face and alternately closing each eye — notice how the finger appears to jump sideways.

Convergence is the way both eyes turn inward (converge) to focus on a nearby object. The closer the object, the more the eyes must converge. The brain detects the muscular effort involved in converging and uses this as information about how close the object is. When you focus on something very close — the end of your own nose, for example — you can feel the slight strain of convergence. For objects far away, almost no convergence is needed.

Monocular Versus Binocular Cues: Key Differences

A useful way to remember the distinction between monocular and binocular cues is to consider what each type depends on. Monocular cues are properties of the visual scene itself — they are present in the pattern of light that reaches the retina and work even in a photograph or painting. This is why artists can create a convincing sense of depth on a flat canvas using linear perspective, relative size and occlusion. You do not need two eyes or a three-dimensional scene to use these cues.

Binocular cues, by contrast, depend on having two eyes that are physically separated. They arise from the geometry of the visual system itself rather than from properties of the scene. Retinal disparity is created by the fact that your eyes are roughly 6–7 centimetres apart; the further apart the viewpoints, the greater the potential disparity for close objects. Convergence is a proprioceptive signal — it comes from muscles in the eye, not from the light pattern.

In practice, the brain uses all available depth cues simultaneously and combines them to produce a single, coherent depth estimate. Binocular cues are particularly useful for judging the distance of close objects (within a few metres), where retinal disparity is largest. Monocular cues remain informative at much greater distances, where the eyes are too far apart for retinal disparity to be measurably different between near and far objects.

Two Theories of Perception

How do we make sense of what we see? There are two major competing theories. Gibson argues that the visual environment contains all the information we need to perceive directly, without any need to draw on memory or past experience. Gregory argues the opposite: that perception is an active, inference-based process built from prior knowledge. This lesson covers Gibson’s direct theory. Understanding which side of this debate each theory belongs to is essential — it maps directly onto the nature–nurture debate in psychology.

Key Fact

Gibson’s direct theory is a nature account: it argues the visual world provides enough information for direct perception without the need for learned inference or prior knowledge. Perception is driven from the bottom up — by the richness of the environment rather than by what we already know.

Gibson’s Direct Theory of Perception

James Gibson proposed that the real world is rich enough in visual information that we can perceive it directly, without needing to make inferences or use memory. The environment contains all the information the visual system needs; the brain does not need to add extra interpretation on top of it.

Gibson emphasised that in everyday life, perception happens in a dynamic, moving world. When you move through space, the visual scene changes in complex but structured ways — textures become denser in the distance, objects change in size, and the flow of the visual scene shifts in predictable patterns around the direction you are moving. Gibson called this rich, changing flow of information the optic array. He argued that the optic array alone contains sufficient information for accurate perception.

Bottom-Up Processing

Gibson’s account is described as bottom-up processing. Perception starts at the bottom — with the raw sensory input — and builds upward to a complete perception. Nothing needs to be added from memory or experience; the environment does the work. This contrasts with Gregory’s top-down approach, in which prior knowledge and expectations are imposed from the top down onto incoming sensory data.

The Role of Motion Parallax

One of the most important pieces of information in the moving optic array is motion parallax. When you move your head or travel through space, nearby objects appear to move quickly and in the opposite direction to your own movement, while distant objects appear to move slowly and in the same direction as your movement. This difference in apparent speed provides direct, unambiguous information about depth and distance — no inference needed.

A classic example of motion parallax in action is looking out of a moving train. Trees close to the track rush past rapidly, while distant hills seem to glide slowly in the same direction as the train. Your visual system detects this difference and uses it directly to judge the distance of objects in the scene.

Key Fact

Motion parallax is the difference in the apparent speed and direction of movement of near versus far objects as an observer moves. Near objects appear to move quickly in the opposite direction; far objects appear to move slowly in the same direction. Gibson argued this is direct information in the optic array, requiring no inference.

A strength of Gibson’s theory is that it has high ecological validity. It was developed from observations of real-world perception — particularly from Gibson’s research on pilots’ visual guidance during landing. The theory describes how perception works in the natural environments where it evolved, rather than in artificial laboratory conditions.

A further strength is that the theory accounts well for the speed and accuracy of everyday perception. We navigate the physical world quickly and without effort, which suggests the visual system may indeed be picking up information directly from the environment rather than constructing a complex inferred representation each time.

A weakness is that Gibson’s theory struggles to explain visual illusions. If perception is driven entirely by information in the environment, why do we perceive things that are not there, or misjudge sizes? Illusions suggest the brain is doing more than passively picking up information — it is actively constructing perception in ways that can go wrong. Gregory’s constructivist theory handles illusions better.

Another weakness is that the theory does not fully account for the role of experience. Research on people who have their vision restored after early blindness (such as the patient S.B., studied by Gregory and Wallace) shows they struggle to perceive depth and form, suggesting prior experience does play a role in building perceptual ability.
