content_html:
Gregory’s Constructivist Theory

While Gibson argued that the visual environment provides all the information needed for direct perception, Richard Gregory disagreed. Gregory proposed the constructivist theory of perception, which argues that perception is an active process of construction. The brain uses incoming sensory information together with prior knowledge and past experience to build (“construct”) a best-guess interpretation of the world. Gregory argued the sensory data reaching the eyes is often incomplete or ambiguous, and the brain fills in the gaps using what it already knows.

Key Fact

Gregory’s constructivist theory is a nurture account: perception is built from inferences drawn from both sensory cues and past experience. It is a top-down process — knowledge and expectation are applied from above to interpret the incoming sensory data from below.

Top-Down Processing

Gregory’s approach is described as top-down processing. Prior knowledge and context act as hypotheses: the brain generates a “best guess” about what is out there, tests it against the incoming sensory data, and settles on the interpretation that fits best. Usually this works efficiently. But sometimes the brain’s best guess turns out to be wrong — and the result is a visual illusion.

Visual Illusions and What They Tell Us

Visual illusions are cases where our perception of a stimulus does not match the physical reality of that stimulus. For Gregory, illusions are not failures of the visual system; they are evidence that perception is an inferential process. When the brain’s inference is wrong, an illusion is the result. There are four main explanations for why illusions occur:

Ambiguity — some stimuli can be interpreted in more than one way. The brain fluctuates between competing interpretations. Misinterpreted depth cues — the brain incorrectly applies depth cues to a two-dimensional image, creating an inaccurate size or distance judgement. Fiction — the brain perceives shapes or contours that are not actually present in the image. Size constancy — the brain automatically adjusts the perceived size of an object based on apparent distance, which can lead to misjudgement.

The Ponzo illusion presents two identical horizontal lines placed between two converging lines (like railway tracks). The upper line looks longer, even though both are the same length. Gregory’s explanation: the converging lines trigger linear perspective depth cues, making the upper line appear further away. Because of size constancy, an object that appears further away but projects the same retinal image must be perceived as physically larger.

The Müller-Lyer illusion shows two equal lines: one with arrow fins pointing inward, one with fins pointing outward. The inward-fin line appears shorter than the outward-fin line. Gregory’s explanation: the arrow fins resemble the inside corner of a room (inward, appearing further away) or the outside corner of a building (outward, appearing closer). Size constancy then adjusts perceived size in line with apparent depth.

Rubin’s vase is an ambiguous figure: the same image can be seen as either a white vase against a dark background, or two dark faces in profile looking at each other. The perception flips between these two interpretations because the brain cannot settle on a single best-guess for which region is “figure” and which is “ground.” This illustrates the ambiguity explanation of illusions.

The Ames Room is a specially constructed room that appears to be a normal rectangular room when viewed through a peephole, but is actually a distorted shape with one corner much further away and lower than the other. Because the brain applies the size constancy principle using misinterpreted depth cues, two people of the same height standing in opposite corners appear to be very different sizes.

The Kanizsa triangle places three “pac-man” shapes arranged so the brain perceives a bright white triangle in the centre — yet no triangle is actually drawn. This is a fiction illusion: the brain constructs a contour that does not exist because this is the most sensible interpretation of the partial shapes.

The Necker cube is a wire-frame drawing of a cube with no depth cues to determine which face is in front. The brain flips between two interpretations of which face is facing outward and which is facing inward. Like Rubin’s vase, this shows ambiguity: without enough information to fix on one interpretation, the brain alternates between equally plausible best guesses.

Evaluating Gregory’s Constructivist Theory

A major strength of Gregory’s theory is that it provides a coherent explanation for visual illusions — something Gibson’s direct theory struggles with. If perception involves inference from prior knowledge, it follows that the brain can construct incorrect perceptions when its inferences are based on misleading cues.

A weakness is that top-down processing is harder to study scientifically than bottom-up processing. It is difficult to isolate the effect of prior knowledge because everyone’s experience differs. The theory also does not fully explain why perception is so often accurate — if it relies on error-prone inferences, we might expect more mistakes than we actually experience in everyday perception.

Key Fact

Six named illusions to know: Ponzo and Müller-Lyer (misinterpreted depth cues + size constancy); Rubin’s vase and the Necker cube (ambiguity); Kanizsa triangle (fiction); Ames Room (misinterpreted depth cues + size constancy). Each is evidence that perception involves inference.

What Is Perceptual Set?

You don’t always see what is actually there. What you perceive depends partly on what you are expecting, what you want, how you feel, and the cultural world you grew up in. Psychologists call this tendency perceptual set. Think of perceptual set as a mental predisposition that influences which features of a scene you pay attention to and how you interpret what you see. It links directly to Gregory’s constructivist theory: the “top-down” factors that shape our perceptual hypotheses include all the factors that create perceptual set.

Key Fact

Perceptual set is influenced by four factors: culture (what we have grown up seeing), motivation (what we want or need), emotion (our current emotional state), and expectation (what the context leads us to anticipate). All four illustrate how top-down processing shapes what we perceive.

Culture and Perception

People raised in different cultural environments develop different perceptual sets. Those who grow up in environments dominated by straight lines, corners, and rectangular buildings — what psychologists call a “carpentered environment” — are more susceptible to certain visual illusions (such as the Müller-Lyer) than those from non-carpentered environments. The brain uses patterns it has seen repeatedly to make perceptual inferences, so culture shapes which patterns become default interpretive frameworks. Research has found that people from cultures with limited exposure to rectangular architecture are less susceptible to some depth-cue-based illusions.

Motivation and Perception

Motivation affects what we notice in a scene. When we have a strong need or desire, we are more likely to perceive things related to that need. A hungry person may notice food cues more readily; a thirsty person may rate pictures of drinks as appearing larger or more vivid than a person who is not thirsty. This suggests that our physiological and psychological drives create a set that prioritises need-relevant stimuli.

Gilchrist and Nesberg’s Study of Motivation

The key named study on motivation and perception is Gilchrist and Nesberg’s. You need to know it in full: aim, method, results, and conclusion.

Key Fact

Gilchrist and Nesberg: Aim — to investigate whether motivation affects perception. Method — participants who had gone without food or water for varying lengths of time were shown images of food and drink and asked to adjust the brightness of the images to match what they had seen. Results — hungrier and thirstier participants adjusted the brightness of food and drink images to appear brighter than less deprived participants did. Conclusion — motivation (physiological need) affects perception, causing need-relevant stimuli to appear more vivid.

Emotion and Expectation

Emotional state also creates a perceptual set. Someone who is anxious may perceive ambiguous stimuli as threatening; someone in a positive mood may interpret the same stimulus more positively. Emotion directs attention toward mood-congruent information, shaping what is noticed and how it is interpreted.

Expectation is perhaps the most directly top-down factor. When the context of a scene creates a strong expectation, the brain is primed to perceive what it expects, even if the stimulus is ambiguous. You have probably misread a word in a text because the sentence context led you to expect a particular word — your brain filled in what was “supposed” to be there.

Bruner and Minturn’s Study of Perceptual Set

Bruner and Minturn investigated how expectation shapes perception using an ambiguous stimulus — a figure that could be seen as either the letter “B” or the number “13” depending on how it was read.

Key Fact

Bruner and Minturn: Aim — to investigate whether context (expectation) affects perception of an ambiguous figure. Method — participants were shown either a series of letters or a series of numbers before being shown an ambiguous figure (could be “B” or “13”). Results — participants shown letters perceived the figure as “B”; participants shown numbers perceived it as “13.” Conclusion — prior context creates an expectation (perceptual set) that determines how an ambiguous stimulus is perceived.

A strength of research into factors affecting perception is that both studies used controlled experimental methods. Bruner and Minturn’s study manipulated context (letter series vs number series) as the independent variable and measured perception of the ambiguous figure as the dependent variable — this gives high internal validity because extraneous variables were controlled. Gilchrist and Nesberg similarly manipulated food/water deprivation levels systematically.

A weakness is that laboratory studies of perceptual set may have limited ecological validity. The stimuli used (simple letters, images of food) are artificial and may not reflect how motivation or expectation affect perception in complex, real-world settings. Individual differences — in culture, personality, and prior experience — mean that findings may not generalise to all people equally.

The Developing Brain

You started life as a single cell. Within weeks of conception, a simple tube of neural tissue had formed, and from this beginning every thought you have ever had, every skill you have ever learned, grew. Understanding how the brain builds itself — and what shapes that process — sits at the heart of developmental psychology.

Brain development follows a pattern that moves from the simplest, most essential structures through to the most complex. The brain does not switch on all at once; it assembles itself in layers, with the parts that keep you alive forming first and the parts that allow you to think, reason and create developing last. This ordering is not random — it reflects millions of years of evolution prioritising survival over sophisticated cognition.

Simple Neural Structures in the Womb

In the first weeks after conception the embryo develops a neural tube. This structure closes and begins to swell at one end, forming the basic regions of the brain. By the time a baby is born, these regions have become far more elaborate, but their foundations were laid before the second trimester had even begun.

The brain develops from the bottom upwards and from the inside outwards. The innermost, oldest structures form first; the outer, newer structures form last. Psychologists describe four key regions in the order they typically mature: the brain stem, the thalamus, the cerebellum, and the cortex.

Key Fact

Brain development follows a bottom-up sequence: brain stem (autonomic functions), thalamus (sensory processing), cerebellum (movement coordination) and cortex (higher cognition). Each layer builds on the one below it.

The Brain Stem: Keeping Alive

The brain stem is the most primitive structure, and it develops first. It controls autonomic functions — the processes that keep you alive without you having to think about them. Breathing, heart rate, blood pressure, swallowing and the sleep–wake cycle are all regulated here. A newborn baby’s brain stem is functional from birth, which is why they breathe, cry and sleep even though the rest of their brain is still immature.

The Thalamus: Routing Sensory Information

Above the brain stem sits the thalamus. It matures next and acts as the brain’s central switchboard for sensory processing. Almost all sensory signals — from your eyes, ears, skin and tongue — are routed through the thalamus before reaching the cortex for interpretation. Without a functioning thalamus, even a fully developed cortex could not receive the information it needs to make sense of the world.

This is why newborns respond quickly to touch, sound and light even before they can make sense of what they are experiencing. The thalamus is relaying the signals; it is the cortex — still developing — that will eventually interpret them fully.

The cerebellum sits at the back of the brain below the cortex. It is responsible for coordinating movement and balance. When a child learns to walk, the cerebellum is doing the heavy lifting — gradually building a smooth, coordinated programme of movement from what was initially a stumbling series of adjustments. The cerebellum also plays a role in procedural skills: riding a bike, typing and catching a ball all rely on cerebellar coordination.

The cerebellum continues to develop into early childhood, which is why babies cannot walk immediately after birth. Even in adulthood, damage to the cerebellum causes difficulties with balance and coordination rather than with thinking or memory — confirming how precisely localised its function is.

The Cortex: Thinking and Cognition

The outermost layer of the brain is the cortex. It is the last structure to develop and the one that develops for the longest time — the prefrontal cortex, which handles planning and decision-making, does not fully mature until a person’s mid-twenties. The cortex is responsible for higher-order cognition: language, abstract thinking, problem-solving, creativity and conscious perception.

Because the cortex develops so late and over such a long period, it is the part of the brain most shaped by experience after birth. This has important implications for education: the brain is not a finished product at birth but a work in progress that continues to be built by the experiences a child has.

Key Fact

The cortex is responsible for higher cognition — language, reasoning and problem-solving — and is the last region to mature. Its prolonged development means it is the part of the brain most open to being shaped by learning and experience after birth.

The debate about nature versus nurture asks how much of our development is determined by our genes (nature) and how much by our environment and experiences (nurture). In brain development, both play essential roles.

The nature side of the argument points to the fact that the basic sequence of brain development — brain stem first, cortex last — is the same in all humans. Genes direct the initial construction: which neurons form, how they connect and what functions they serve. This blueprint is inherited.

The nurture side points to the fact that the brain is not a static structure. Neurons that are stimulated by experience form stronger connections (synapses), while those that are not used weaken or disappear — a process called synaptic pruning. Language development offers a clear example: babies are born with the capacity to learn any language, but they will only acquire the specific language(s) they hear around them. The environment shapes which neural pathways are strengthened.

Most psychologists today accept that brain development is an interaction of both nature and nurture. Genes set the parameters; experience fills in the detail. Neither alone can fully explain how the human brain becomes what it is.

Why Do Children Think Differently?

Have you ever tried to explain something straightforward to a young child, only to find they seem to be reasoning from a completely different set of rules? The Swiss psychologist Jean Piaget argued that this was not a question of children knowing less — it was a question of children thinking differently. His Theory of Cognitive Development, first published in the twentieth century, proposed that intelligence itself develops in stages, each qualitatively different from the last.

Piaget’s approach was distinctive because he did not just measure what children knew; he investigated how they reasoned. By observing his own children and later running systematic experiments, he identified a pattern of development that he believed was universal — applying to all children, regardless of culture or background.

Schemas, Assimilation and Accommodation

Central to Piaget’s theory is the idea that we build knowledge through mental frameworks called schemas. A very young child might have a simple schema for ‘dog’ — a four-legged animal. When they encounter a new dog, they recognise it using this existing schema. This process of fitting new experience into an existing schema is called assimilation.

But what if the child then encounters a cat? It is also four-legged, but clearly different from a dog. Their existing ‘dog’ schema does not quite fit, so they must adjust or create a new schema. This process of changing or creating schemas to fit new information is called accommodation. Together, assimilation and accommodation drive cognitive development: the child is constantly trying to make sense of the world, either fitting new experience into existing ideas or restructuring their thinking to accommodate it.

Key Fact

Assimilation = fitting new information into an existing schema. Accommodation = changing or creating a schema to fit new information. Both processes work together to develop intelligence through Piaget’s four stages.

The Four Stages of Development

Piaget proposed that all children pass through four stages in the same order. The age ranges are approximate, but the sequence is fixed — a child cannot reach a later stage without passing through the earlier ones.

In the sensorimotor stage (approximately 0 to 2 years), infants explore the world through their senses and physical movements. They do not yet have language or symbolic thought. A key development in this stage is object permanence — the understanding that objects still exist even when they are out of sight. Before this develops, a young infant who watches a toy being hidden will simply stop looking for it, as if it has ceased to exist. Once object permanence is established, the child will actively search for the hidden toy.

In the pre-operational stage (2 to 7 years), children develop language and can use symbols, but their thinking has important limitations. They are egocentric — they see the world only from their own perspective and assume others see, think and feel exactly as they do. They also lack conservation — the ability to understand that quantity stays the same when appearance changes. Pour water from a short wide glass into a tall thin glass, and a pre-operational child will say there is now more water, even though they watched the same amount being poured.

In the concrete operational stage (7 to 11 years), children develop logical thought but only when applied to real, tangible objects and situations. They master conservation and become less egocentric — they begin to appreciate that other people can have different perspectives. However, they still struggle with purely abstract reasoning. If you ask a concrete operational child a logic puzzle with no physical objects (pure hypothetical reasoning), they will find it difficult.

In the formal operational stage (11 years onwards), adolescents develop the capacity for abstract thinking — they can reason about hypothetical situations, plan ahead and think about possibilities, not just actualities. This is the stage at which a student can engage with algebraic reasoning, philosophical debate, and complex ‘what if’ questions. Piaget believed this was the highest stage of cognitive development and that not all adults necessarily reach it fully.

Evaluating Piaget’s Theory

Piaget’s theory has been enormously influential, but it has also been challenged. Critics argue that he underestimated children’s abilities at each stage — later studies (including by McGarrigle and Donaldson, and Hughes) found that when tasks were made more child-friendly, younger children could demonstrate abilities Piaget thought were beyond them. His methods often involved clinical conversations with children, and some researchers argued that the way questions were phrased confused children rather than revealing their true abilities.

Key Fact

Piaget’s four stages in order: sensorimotor (0–2, object permanence), pre-operational (2–7, egocentric, lacks conservation), concrete operational (7–11, logical with real objects, gains conservation), formal operational (11+, abstract reasoning). The sequence is fixed; the ages are approximate.

lesson_title: Piaget in Education: Conservation and Egocentrism
content_html:
Piaget in the Classroom

Piaget’s theory was not just an academic description of how children think — it had direct implications for education. If children at different ages are genuinely incapable of certain types of reasoning, then teaching them content that requires that reasoning is pointless. Piaget’s key educational message was: match what you teach to the stage of thinking the child has actually reached.

This influenced how schools are designed and how teachers plan lessons. Primary school classrooms with hands-on materials, practical activities and discovery learning all reflect Piaget’s insight that children at the concrete operational stage learn best through interaction with real objects, not through abstract explanation alone.

Egocentrism and Its Reduction

In the pre-operational stage, children are egocentric. This does not mean they are selfish — it means they genuinely cannot take the perspective of another person. Piaget demonstrated this with his ‘Three Mountains Task’, in which children were asked to describe what a doll placed on the other side of a model mountain range would see. Pre-operational children consistently described what they themselves could see, not what the doll’s position would show.

As children move into the concrete operational stage, egocentrism gradually reduces. They begin to understand that other people have different viewpoints, feelings and knowledge. This has important educational implications: collaborative group work, debate and perspective-taking activities become possible and valuable once children reach this stage.

Key Fact

Egocentrism (the inability to take another’s perspective) is characteristic of the pre-operational stage (2–7 years). It reduces as the child enters the concrete operational stage (7–11 years), enabling collaborative and perspective-taking activities in education.

The Development of Conservation

Conservation is the understanding that quantity does not change just because appearance does. Pre-operational children fail conservation tasks — they say a tall thin glass contains more water than a short wide glass even after watching the same water being poured between the two. They focus on the height of the water (what they can see) rather than reasoning about quantity.

Piaget believed children could not reliably pass conservation tasks until the concrete operational stage. In education, this means that until around age seven, lessons should not assume children understand that number, volume or mass are preserved across changes in arrangement or appearance.

McGarrigle and Donaldson’s naughty teddy study directly challenged Piaget’s claims about conservation. The aim was to investigate whether pre-operational children could demonstrate conservation when the change in arrangement was made accidentally rather than intentionally by an adult.

Method: Children aged between 4 and 6 were shown two rows of counters that were the same length. In the standard Piaget condition, the experimenter deliberately spread out one row and asked if there were now more counters. In the naughty teddy condition, a toy teddy ‘accidentally’ scattered one of the rows, and the same question was asked.

Results: In the standard condition, most children gave the incorrect answer (saying the longer row had more counters — matching Piaget’s findings). But in the naughty teddy condition, a much higher proportion of children gave the correct answer, saying the number was still the same.

Conclusion: McGarrigle and Donaldson concluded that Piaget had underestimated children’s conservation ability. When the change was accidental and natural, younger children could conserve — suggesting the issue was with Piaget’s task design rather than with the children’s cognitive capacity. The deliberate act of the experimenter spreading the counters may have signalled to children that something had changed, leading them to give the wrong answer.

Hughes’ policeman doll study challenged Piaget’s claims about egocentrism. The aim was to test whether pre-operational children could take another’s perspective when the task was made more meaningful and understandable.

Method: Hughes used a model with walls dividing it into sections, and placed two toy policemen dolls at various positions. He asked children to hide a boy doll so that neither policeman could see it. The task required the child to take the visual perspective of both policemen — a more complex perspective-taking challenge than Piaget’s Three Mountains Task, but also more meaningful because it had a real narrative purpose.

Results: Most of the children successfully hid the boy doll where neither policeman could see it, demonstrating that they could take the perspectives of the two policemen — something Piaget’s theory predicted they should not be able to do at this age.

Conclusion: Hughes concluded that pre-operational children are less egocentric than Piaget claimed. When the task is meaningful and involves a familiar scenario (hiding from a policeman), even young children can take another’s perspective. This suggests Piaget’s Three Mountains Task was too abstract and unfamiliar, leading to an underestimate of children’s abilities.

Key Fact

Both McGarrigle and Donaldson (naughty teddy) and Hughes (policeman doll) found that children showed conservation and perspective-taking ability earlier than Piaget claimed, when tasks were made more natural and meaningful. Both studies challenge the idea that children’s thinking is as limited as Piaget’s original tasks suggested.

Implications for Education

The findings of McGarrigle and Donaldson, and Hughes, have important implications for how we understand and apply Piaget in education. If children are more capable than Piaget’s original tasks suggested, then earlier introduction of collaborative and perspective-based activities may be appropriate. However, Piaget’s core educational insight remains valid: the cognitive demands of a lesson should be matched to where the child actually is developmentally, not where a teacher assumes they should be.

Can You Change How Smart You Are?

Some people believe that intelligence is fixed — you are born with a certain amount and that is it. Others believe that with effort and the right strategies, you can always improve. These are not just personal opinions: psychologist Carol Dweck argued that which belief you hold has a profound effect on how you learn, how you respond to failure, and how successful you become. Her theory divides learners into two broad types based on their beliefs about ability.

Dweck’s Mindset Theory

Carol Dweck proposed that learners operate from one of two fundamental beliefs about their intelligence and abilities. These are known as the fixed mindset and the growth mindset.

A person with a fixed mindset believes that you are either good at something or you are not, and that hard work cannot really change this. Failure is threatening because it feels like evidence of permanent inability. These learners tend to avoid challenges where they might look stupid and are more likely to give up when work gets difficult.

A person with a growth mindset believes that ability and intelligence can be developed through effort, practice and good strategies. Failure is informative — it tells you where to try harder or where to change your approach. These learners tend to embrace challenges, persist in the face of difficulties, and improve more over time.

Key Fact

Fixed mindset: believes ability is unchangeable; avoids challenges; gives up at failure. Growth mindset: believes ability can be developed; embraces challenges; uses failure as information. Dweck’s research found that mindset significantly predicts academic achievement.

The Role of Praise

Dweck’s research found that the type of praise a child receives can shape which mindset they develop. Praising children for being clever or talented (“You’re so smart!”) promotes a fixed mindset: it signals that intelligence is a fixed trait worth protecting, so children avoid challenges where they might not look smart. Praising children for their effort and strategies (“You worked really hard on that”) promotes a growth mindset: it signals that the path to success is through effort, not inherited ability.

This finding has important implications for teachers and parents. Well-intentioned compliments about ability can, paradoxically, reduce a child’s willingness to take on difficult tasks. Effort-based praise is more likely to build resilience and a love of learning.

Self-Efficacy and Learning

Self-efficacy refers to a person’s belief in their own capacity to succeed. It is closely related to mindset: a growth mindset tends to support higher self-efficacy because the learner believes that improvement is possible. A fixed mindset tends to undermine self-efficacy because a student who believes their ability is fixed is more likely to interpret failure as a ceiling on what they can ever achieve.

High self-efficacy is associated with setting more ambitious goals, persisting longer on difficult tasks, and recovering more quickly from setbacks. In educational settings, teachers who help students build accurate beliefs about their ability to improve — through feedback focused on progress — are supporting self-efficacy alongside academic development.

The idea of learning styles became popular in education from the 1970s onwards. The claim is that students learn best when information is delivered in a format matching their preferred style. The simplest version of this idea distinguishes between verbalisers, who prefer to learn through reading and verbal explanation, and visualisers, who prefer images, diagrams and spatial representations.

In practical terms, a verbaliser might prefer detailed written notes and explanations, while a visualiser might prefer concept maps, timelines and visual summaries. Teachers who try to ‘match’ their style to each student’s preference are applying learning styles theory — though, as we will see, this application has been strongly criticised.

Cognitive scientist Daniel Willingham is one of the most prominent critics of learning styles theory. His central argument is that while people may have preferences for how they receive information, preference does not equal effectiveness — and the evidence does not show that teaching in a student’s preferred style produces better learning outcomes.

Willingham argues that whether a visual or verbal presentation works better depends on the nature of the content, not on the student’s preference. Some information is inherently spatial and is best presented visually (maps, diagrams of anatomical structures). Other information is inherently verbal and is best presented in words (arguments, narratives, definitions). The content should drive the format, not the supposed preference of the learner.

Willingham also points out that the ‘meshing hypothesis’ — the idea that matching teaching style to learning style improves outcomes — has not been consistently supported by experimental research. Studies that have tried to test it have typically not found that learners do better when taught in their preferred style.

Key Fact

Willingham argued that learning styles theory is not supported by evidence: preference does not equal effectiveness, the content should determine the format, and experimental research has not consistently shown that matching teaching to preferred style improves outcomes.

Evaluating Mindset Theory and Learning Styles

Dweck’s mindset theory has been broadly supported by research and has been widely applied in schools through ‘growth mindset’ interventions. However, some researchers have questioned whether the effects found in controlled studies translate reliably into real-world classrooms. Replication studies have sometimes found smaller effects than Dweck’s original research.

Learning styles as a concept has intuitive appeal, and people do have real preferences for how they like to receive information. The problem, as Willingham points out, is not that preferences exist but that matching instruction to preference has not been shown to improve learning. The implication for education is to design lessons based on what the content requires and what cognitive science shows works — rather than on unvalidated style categories.

The Starting Point of Scientific Research

Every psychological study starts with a question. A researcher notices something about human behaviour and wants to know why it happens, or whether one thing influences another. But noticing something and testing it scientifically are very different tasks. Before any data can be collected, a researcher must be precise: they must state exactly what they expect to find, define what they are measuring and ensure they have an appropriate group of participants. These steps are the foundation of scientific psychology.

Hypotheses

A hypothesis is a precise, testable prediction. It states in advance what the researcher expects to find. A hypothesis must be operationalised — meaning both the independent variable and the dependent variable must be defined in terms of how they will be measured, not described vaguely.

Compare these two predictions: “People who revise more will do better” versus “Participants who revise using flashcards for five hours will recall more words from a 20-word list than participants who reread their notes for five hours.” The second is a well-operationalised hypothesis because both conditions of the independent variable (flashcards vs rereading) and the dependent variable (words recalled from a 20-word list) are clearly defined and measurable.

Key Fact

A well-operationalised hypothesis states both conditions of the independent variable AND a clearly measurable dependent variable. Without operationalisation, a hypothesis cannot be properly tested, and mark schemes require both elements for full marks.

Null and Alternative Hypotheses

Every study involves two complementary hypotheses. The null hypothesis states that there is no difference or no relationship between the variables — any result found is due to chance. For example: “There will be no significant difference in word recall between participants who revise with flashcards and those who reread notes.”

The alternative hypothesis (also called the experimental hypothesis) states that there will be a difference or relationship — this is what the researcher expects to find. For example: “Participants who revise using flashcards will recall significantly more words from a 20-word list than those who reread their notes.”

Statistical testing after the study will determine whether the data allows the null hypothesis to be rejected. If results are ‘significant’ (unlikely to be due to chance), the null hypothesis is rejected and the alternative hypothesis is supported. Psychologists do not ‘prove’ their hypotheses; they provide evidence for or against them.

A independent variable (IV) is the one the researcher changes or manipulates. In the flashcard example, the IV is the revision method (flashcards vs rereading).

A dependent variable (DV) is what the researcher measures — the outcome. In the flashcard example, the DV is the number of words recalled from the 20-word list.

Extraneous variables are any other variables that could affect the DV that the researcher has not controlled. For example, if one group of participants had a higher baseline memory ability, that could explain any difference in word recall rather than the revision method. Controlling extraneous variables is essential to ensure results reflect the IV rather than something else.

Target Populations and Samples

A researcher almost never studies every member of a group they are interested in. Instead, they select a sample from the target population. The sample should be representative — it should reflect the characteristics of the target population as closely as possible so that conclusions can be generalised beyond the study itself.

Random sampling gives every member of the target population an equal chance of being selected. The researcher lists all members of the population and uses a random process (lottery, random number generator) to select participants. Strength: unbiased and representative. Weakness: requires a complete list of the population, which is often difficult to obtain, and non-responders may create a biased final sample.

Opportunity sampling selects whoever is available and willing to take part. A researcher standing at a university entrance and asking passers-by is using opportunity sampling. Strength: quick, easy and inexpensive. Weakness: biased towards people who are easily available at that time and place, so the sample may not be representative of the target population.

Systematic sampling selects every nth person from a list. For example, if there are 1,000 people in the population and you need 100 participants, you would select every 10th person. Strength: straightforward to carry out and reduces researcher bias. Weakness: may still be biased if the list has a pattern that makes every nth person systematically different.

Stratified sampling divides the population into subgroups (strata) based on relevant characteristics (e.g. age, gender) and then randomly selects participants from each stratum in proportion to their size in the full population. Strength: ensures the sample reflects the population structure, making it highly representative. Weakness: time-consuming and requires detailed knowledge of the population’s structure.

Key Fact

Four sampling methods: random (equal chance, unbiased but hard to obtain full list), opportunity (quick but biased towards available people), systematic (every nth person, straightforward but potential pattern bias), stratified (proportional subgroups, highly representative but time-consuming).

Why Use Experiments?

The experiment is the gold standard of psychological research. When a psychologist wants to establish that one thing causes another — not merely that the two are associated — an experiment is the method that can demonstrate causation. This is because experiments involve directly manipulating one variable while keeping everything else as constant as possible, then measuring the effect on another variable.

The key distinction the spec requires you to understand is between the research method (how the data is gathered) and the experimental design (how participants are allocated to conditions within the experiment). These are two separate decisions a researcher makes. A laboratory experiment can use any of the three experimental designs; so can a field experiment.

Key Fact

Research method = how data is collected (lab, field, natural experiment, observation, questionnaire etc.). Experimental design = how participants are divided between conditions (independent groups, repeated measures or matched pairs). These are distinct decisions — a common exam error is confusing the two.

Experimental Designs

Once a researcher decides to run an experiment, they must choose how to use their participants. There are three main experimental designs.

In an independent groups design, different participants take part in each condition. One group does condition A, a different group does condition B. For example, Group 1 revises with flashcards; Group 2 revises by rereading notes. They are separate, independent groups.

Strength: there are no order effects, because participants only experience one condition. Weakness: individual differences between the groups may affect results (one group might naturally have better memories), and more participants are needed because each person only provides data for one condition.

In a repeated measures design, the same participants take part in all conditions. Every person does condition A and condition B. This eliminates individual differences as a confounding variable, because the same person is compared to themselves.

Strength: individual differences are controlled — each participant acts as their own control. Fewer participants are needed. Weakness: order effects can occur. If participants do condition A first and then condition B, they may perform better on condition B because of practice (‘practice effect’), or worse due to fatigue or boredom. Counterbalancing (half the participants do A then B; the other half do B then A) can reduce order effects.

A matched pairs design pairs participants on a relevant variable (such as age, IQ or previous experience) before assigning one from each pair to each condition. It combines the advantages of independent groups (no order effects) and repeated measures (individual differences partly controlled).

Strength: individual differences are reduced because each pair is similar on the key variable; no order effects because each person only takes part in one condition. Weakness: very time-consuming to match participants carefully; impossible to match on every relevant variable; if one participant drops out, both members of the pair are lost.

Types of Experiment: Laboratory, Field and Natural

As well as choosing a design, a researcher must choose the setting and level of control. The three main types of experiment each involve the manipulation of an independent variable, but they differ in where they take place and how much control the researcher has.

A laboratory experiment takes place in a controlled setting, usually a specially designed room. The researcher can control many variables: lighting, noise, temperature, the exact stimuli presented and so on. Strength: high control means results more clearly reflect the IV; easier to replicate. Weakness: the artificial setting reduces ecological validity — participants may not behave as they would in everyday life.

A field experiment takes place in a real-world setting. The researcher still manipulates the IV but the participants are in their natural environment and may not know they are being studied. Strength: high ecological validity because behaviour occurs in a natural setting. Weakness: less control over extraneous variables; ethical concerns if participants have not consented.

A natural experiment involves a naturally occurring event as the IV — the researcher does not manipulate it but measures the effect of something that has happened independently. Strength: high ecological validity; allows study of variables that would be unethical to manipulate deliberately. Weakness: low control; participants cannot be randomly allocated to conditions because the IV was not chosen by the researcher.

Choosing the Right Design and Method

The choice of experimental design and research method depends on the research question. If a researcher is concerned about order effects and has enough participants, independent groups is the safest design. If individual differences are a major worry and order effects can be counterbalanced, repeated measures is preferable. If the research involves sensitive topics requiring real-world settings — for example, studying helping behaviour in a public space — a field experiment has advantages over a laboratory setting, even though it sacrifices some control.

Key Fact

Three experimental designs: independent groups (different participants per condition — no order effects but individual differences may confound); repeated measures (same participants, controls individual differences but risks order effects); matched pairs (paired on a variable, avoids order effects and reduces individual differences but time-consuming).

Beyond the Experiment

Experiments are powerful tools for establishing causation, but they are not always possible or appropriate. Some questions in psychology cannot be answered experimentally — it would be unethical to manipulate certain variables, or the topic is too complex to reduce to a single controlled setting. For these situations, psychologists use non-experimental methods: interviews, questionnaires, case studies and observation studies. Each has its own strengths and weaknesses, and each is suited to different kinds of research questions.

Quantitative and Qualitative Methods

Non-experimental methods can produce either quantitative data (numerical results, such as scores, frequencies or percentages) or qualitative data (detailed descriptions of experience, such as what participants say or how they behave). Most methods can produce either, depending on how they are used — a questionnaire can include both numerical rating scales (quantitative) and open-ended questions inviting longer responses (qualitative).

An interview involves a researcher asking questions and recording the participant’s responses. Interviews can be structured (every participant asked the same predetermined questions in the same order, producing quantitative data) or unstructured (open conversation following the participant’s responses, producing rich qualitative data).

Strength of interviews: they can explore complex experiences in depth; unstructured interviews allow unexpected themes to emerge. Weakness: interviewer bias — the researcher’s manner, appearance or phrasing can influence participant responses; time-consuming and difficult to analyse consistently, especially unstructured data.

A questionnaire is a set of written questions completed by participants, often without the researcher present. Questions can be closed (ticking a box, rating on a scale — produces quantitative data) or open (written response — produces qualitative data).

Strength: large numbers of participants can be reached cheaply and quickly; no interviewer bias if completed independently; easy to analyse if questions are closed. Weakness: participants may not answer honestly (social desirability bias — giving the answer they think they should give rather than their true answer); ambiguous questions can be interpreted differently; low response rates may produce a biased sample.

A case study is an in-depth investigation of a single individual, group or event. It typically uses a combination of methods (interviews, observation, psychometric tests) to build a detailed picture of the case. Case studies are particularly useful when the case is unusual or extreme — for example, studying an individual with a rare neurological condition to understand normal brain function by contrast.

Strength: provides rich, detailed qualitative data that captures complexity; unique cases can generate hypotheses for further research; can study variables that could not be manipulated experimentally. Weakness: findings cannot be generalised to other people because the case may be unique; the researcher may develop a subjective attachment to the participant; results are not replicable.

In an observation study, the researcher watches and records participants’ behaviour without manipulating any variables. Observations can be naturalistic (watching behaviour in its natural setting) or structured (in a controlled setting with predetermined categories to record).

A key technical requirement of observation studies is using categories of behaviour — a predetermined list of specific, clearly defined behaviours to record (e.g. ‘number of times participant initiates conversation’ rather than ‘social behaviour’). This makes data more objective and consistent.

Interobserver reliability is a crucial check: two or more observers independently record the same behaviour, and their records are compared. High agreement indicates the observation categories are clear and consistently applicable. Strength: naturalistic observations have high ecological validity. Weakness: observer bias — what one person notices may differ from another; participants who know they are being watched may behave differently (Hawthorne effect).

Correlation

A correlation measures the association between two variables. It tells us whether, as one variable increases, the other tends to increase (positive correlation), decrease (negative correlation) or show no consistent pattern (no correlation).

Correlations are displayed using scatter diagrams. Each participant provides two scores (one for each variable), which are plotted as a single dot on the graph. A positive correlation produces dots trending from bottom-left to top-right. A negative correlation produces dots trending from top-left to bottom-right. A weak or no correlation produces a scattered cluster with no clear trend.

Key Fact

A correlation shows association, not causation. Two variables may be strongly correlated because a third, unmeasured variable causes both. This is called a third variable problem. For example, ice cream sales and drowning rates both increase in summer, but ice cream does not cause drowning — hot weather (the third variable) drives both.

Strengths and Weaknesses of Correlations

Strength: correlations allow researchers to study the relationship between variables that cannot be manipulated ethically (e.g. the association between stress and illness). They are also useful as a starting point for identifying patterns that may be worth investigating with a controlled experiment.

Weakness: correlations cannot establish causation. Because neither variable is manipulated, we cannot conclude that one variable causes the other. This is the most important limitation of correlational research.

Key Fact

Non-experimental methods summary: interviews (verbal, structured or unstructured), questionnaires (written, closed or open), case studies (in-depth single case), observations (behaviour categories, interobserver reliability checked). None of these establish causation — only a controlled experiment can do that.

Designing Research That Works

Collecting data is only valuable if the data accurately reflects what you intended to measure. Two fundamental concepts underpin the quality of any psychological study: reliability and validity. Beyond quality, research involving human participants also carries ethical responsibilities — and in the UK, these are set out by the British Psychological Society (BPS).

Standardised Procedures

A key way to improve reliability is to use standardised procedures. This means every participant experiences exactly the same conditions: the same instructions, the same environment, the same timing, the same stimuli. Without standardisation, differences between participants’ performance could reflect differences in how the study was conducted rather than genuine variation in the variable being measured.

Standardised instructions to participants are a core part of this. Written instructions ensure that every participant receives identical information before the study begins. The researcher delivers the same briefing — or participants read the same text — regardless of who is conducting the session. This also means that if another researcher wants to replicate the study, they can follow the same procedure and expect comparable results.

Key Fact

Reliability = consistency (getting the same result each time the study is run under the same conditions). Validity = accuracy (measuring what you actually intend to measure, in a way that reflects real behaviour). A study can be reliable without being valid: for example, a memory test that consistently scores the same people highly may be measuring intelligence rather than memory.

Randomisation and Allocation to Conditions

Randomisation refers to using chance to allocate participants to conditions. In an independent groups design, random allocation means each participant has an equal chance of being placed in condition A or condition B. This controls for individual differences between conditions — it reduces the risk that one group is systematically different from the other in a way that could affect results.

Randomisation can also be used to determine the order in which stimuli are presented (for example, if a researcher is testing memory for a list of words, the order in which the words appear should be randomised to prevent order from affecting which words are recalled).

Counterbalancing is used in repeated measures designs to reduce order effects. When the same participants take part in multiple conditions, there is a risk that their performance in later conditions is affected by having already done earlier ones — either improved by practice or reduced by fatigue. Counterbalancing divides participants so that half do condition A then condition B (AB order), and the other half do condition B then condition A (BA order). If any order effect exists, it is spread equally across both conditions and cancels out.

Counterbalancing is distinct from randomisation of stimuli. It specifically addresses the sequence of experimental conditions when participants take part in all of them.

Extraneous Variables and Controlling Them

Any variable that could affect the dependent variable other than the independent variable is an extraneous variable. If not controlled, extraneous variables become confounding variables — they provide an alternative explanation for any difference found between conditions. Researchers control extraneous variables through standardised procedures, random allocation, controlled settings, and matched pairs or repeated measures designs.

Reliability and Validity in Research Planning

When planning research, psychologists consider reliability and validity at every stage. Sampling methods affect external validity (how well results generalise to the target population) — a biased sample reduces it. Experimental designs affect internal validity — poor control of extraneous variables means the IV may not be the real cause of any difference found. Quantitative and qualitative methods differ in their reliability and validity trade-offs: quantitative data is more reliable and easier to compare, but may miss the depth and meaning of experience; qualitative data captures richer detail but is harder to replicate consistently.

Psychological research involves human participants, which creates ethical responsibilities. The BPS sets out guidelines that researchers must follow. Key ethical issues include informed consent — participants must be told what the study involves and agree to take part freely, without pressure. They have the right to withdraw at any point without penalty.

Confidentiality means that participants’ personal data must be kept private and not shared without consent. Protection from harm requires researchers to ensure no lasting physical or psychological damage results from participation. After the study, a debrief must be provided: participants are told the full purpose of the study and are given the chance to ask questions or withdraw their data.

Where deception has been used (withholding the true purpose to prevent demand characteristics), the debrief is especially important. Deception should only be used if it is unavoidable and it must not cause participants lasting distress. The right to withdraw data after the study is part of the debrief process.

Key Fact

The BPS ethical guidelines require: informed consent (explain study, get agreement), right to withdraw (can leave at any time, no penalty), confidentiality (data kept anonymous), protection from harm (no lasting physical or psychological damage), and debrief (full explanation after the study, option to withdraw data).

Working with Data

Collecting data is only the beginning. Once a psychologist has run a study, they must organise, summarise and display the results in a way that makes patterns visible and allows conclusions to be drawn. Data handling and descriptive statistics are the tools that do this work. They run through every topic in psychology — understanding them unlocks your ability to interpret any study you encounter.

Types of Data

Quantitative data is expressed as numbers. It allows direct comparison and statistical calculation — for example, the number of words recalled in a memory test, a score on an anxiety rating scale, or the time taken to complete a task. Qualitative data is expressed in words or descriptions. It captures meaning, experience and complexity that numbers cannot convey — for example, a participant’s account of what they were thinking during an experiment.

Both types have value. Quantitative data is easier to compare, analyse statistically and replicate. Qualitative data is richer and more contextual but harder to analyse consistently and more open to researcher interpretation.

Primary and Secondary Data

Primary data is collected directly by the researcher for their own study — running an experiment, conducting an interview, carrying out an observation. It is tailored to the research question and provides the most direct evidence, but is time-consuming and expensive to collect.

Secondary data is data collected previously by someone else, often for a different purpose, that the researcher re-analyses. Examples include published statistics, previously conducted studies, or databases. Strength: saves time and resources. Weakness: the data may not perfectly match the current research question, and the researcher cannot control its quality.

Key Fact

Four data types: quantitative (numbers), qualitative (words/descriptions), primary (collected first-hand by this researcher), secondary (collected previously by someone else). Both quantitative and qualitative can be primary or secondary — these are separate classifications.

Descriptive Statistics: Measures of Central Tendency

Descriptive statistics summarise data concisely. The three main measures of central tendency each give a different picture of the ‘average’ in a dataset.

The mean is calculated by adding all values and dividing by the number of values. For example, if five participants recalled 7, 8, 6, 9 and 5 words, the mean is $$\frac{7+8+6+9+5}{5} = \frac{35}{5} = 7$$ words. The mean uses all the data and is sensitive to outliers — a single extreme value can pull the mean up or down significantly.

The median is the middle value when data is arranged in order. If there is an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values. The median is not affected by outliers, making it a better measure of typical performance when extreme scores are present.

The mode is the most frequently occurring value. It is the only measure that can be used with categorical data (e.g. the most common eye colour in a sample) but gives limited information if every value occurs equally often.

Range

The range describes how spread out the data is. It is calculated by subtracting the lowest value from the highest. For the dataset 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, the range is \(9 - 5 = 4\). A large range indicates great variability in the data; a small range indicates participants performed similarly. Like the mean, the range is sensitive to outliers — one extreme value will inflate it.

Key Fact

Mean = sum of all values ÷ number of values. Median = middle value in ordered data. Mode = most frequent value. Range = highest minus lowest. Mean and range are sensitive to outliers; median is not.

Displaying Quantitative Data

Data is often displayed visually to make patterns clearer. Frequency tables show how many times each value (or range of values) occurs. A bar chart uses separate bars to represent each category; gaps between the bars show that the categories are discrete. A histogram is used for continuous data (such as ages or heights grouped into ranges), with no gaps between bars because the underlying scale is continuous.

Many psychological variables, when measured in large populations, form a normal distribution. This produces a symmetrical, bell-shaped curve when data is plotted. The key characteristics of a normal distribution are: the mean, median and mode are all the same value (the centre of the curve); the distribution is symmetrical about this central point; most scores cluster around the mean, with fewer and fewer scores as you move towards the extremes.

Intelligence test scores and height are classic examples: most people score near the average, with progressively fewer people at the extremes. The normal distribution is important in psychology because many statistical tests assume data is approximately normally distributed, and because it provides a reference for understanding how typical or unusual any given score is. A score at the extreme tail of the distribution is rare; a score near the centre is typical. This is why psychologists often use the normal distribution as a benchmark when evaluating individual results.

What Is Conformity?

Conformity happens when a person changes their behaviour or belief to match the majority of a group. We often conform without being ordered to — we simply go along with the people around us. Think about a time you stayed quiet when you disagreed with everyone else, or copied how others dressed to fit in. That is conformity in action.

Conformity to majority influence is one of the most studied topics in social psychology. Researchers want to understand why people go along with the crowd even when they suspect the crowd is wrong. Two categories of factors shape conformity: social factors (features of the situation) and dispositional factors (features of the individual).

Social Factors Affecting Conformity

Social factors are things about the social situation that push a person towards or away from conforming. Three key social factors are group size, anonymity and task difficulty.

Group size affects conformity because a larger majority creates more social pressure. The effect grows as the group gets bigger, but eventually levels off — adding more people beyond a certain number does not keep increasing conformity. A group of three or four creates strong pressure; a group of fifteen does not produce much more pressure than a group of seven.

Anonymity reduces conformity. When people can respond privately or without being observed by the group, they feel less pressure to match the majority. They are more willing to give their genuine answer. In contrast, when a person must state their answer publicly in front of the group, conformity rises because they want to avoid looking foolish or different.

Task difficulty also matters. When a task is genuinely hard and the correct answer is unclear, people look to others for guidance. This increases conformity because individuals doubt their own judgement. When the task is easy and the answer is obvious, there is less reason to follow the group — though social pressure may still cause some people to conform.

Dispositional Factors Affecting Conformity

Dispositional factors are characteristics of the individual that influence how likely they are to conform. Two key dispositional factors are personality and expertise.

Personality affects conformity in several ways. People who are high in the need for social approval are more likely to conform because they fear rejection. Those with a strong, independent sense of identity may resist group pressure more easily. Confidence in one’s own judgement is also a personality trait that reduces conformity.

Expertise is the other key dispositional factor. Someone who has specialist knowledge in a topic is less likely to conform to the group’s view because they trust their own informed judgement. For example, a trained mechanic hearing a group of non-experts diagnose a car fault is unlikely to agree simply because they are outnumbered. Their expertise gives them confidence to hold their position.

Key Fact

The three social factors affecting conformity are group size, anonymity and task difficulty. The two dispositional factors are personality and expertise. Larger groups, public responses, harder tasks, approval-seeking personalities and lack of expertise all increase conformity.

Asch’s Study of Conformity

Solomon Asch conducted a classic study to test whether people would conform to a clearly wrong majority. His study is one of the most famous in psychology.

Aim: Asch aimed to investigate whether people would conform to the majority view even when the majority was obviously wrong.

Method: Male participants were placed in a room with several other people who were actually confederates (actors working for the researcher). They were shown a card with a standard line and asked to match it to one of three comparison lines of different lengths. The correct answer was always obvious. The confederates had been instructed to give the same wrong answer on 12 out of 18 trials.

Results: Participants gave the wrong answer (matching the majority) on approximately 37% of the critical trials where confederates all gave the wrong answer. Around 75% of participants conformed at least once. When participants responded privately in writing, conformity fell sharply.

Conclusion: Asch concluded that people do conform to majority influence even when the majority is clearly wrong, suggesting that the presence of a unanimous group creates strong social pressure to agree.

Key Fact

In Asch’s conformity study, participants gave wrong answers on around 37% of critical trials, and roughly 75% conformed at least once. When answers were given privately, conformity fell — showing the role of public visibility in creating social pressure.

Evaluating Asch’s Study

Asch’s study has important strengths and weaknesses. A strength is that it was a controlled laboratory experiment, which means the conditions could be carefully controlled and repeated. The use of confederates meant the majority’s behaviour was consistent across trials.

However, there are weaknesses. The sample was limited to male American college students, which means the findings may not apply to women, to other age groups, or to people from different cultures — this reduces generalisability. The artificial lab setting also means the task (comparing line lengths) lacks everyday realism, which reduces ecological validity. Finally, knowing the study involved deception raises ethical concerns about consent, though Asch did debrief participants afterwards.
